report.answer_text:
Access to the President's Daily Brief (PDB) is very tightly restricted.
Regular recipients
Only the President, the Vice President, and a select group of senior officials designated by the President receive the briefing.[1] The president decides who is on that list. It usually includes top national security advisers, though the exact list changes from one administration to the next.
Others who may get access
President-elect: At the president's discretion, the PDB may also be provided to the president-elect between election day and inauguration.[2] By tradition this happens. In 2020, for example, Biden got access later than usual. The delay came because Trump was contesting the election results, and Trump approved the briefings for Biden after the formal transition process was approved.[3]
Former presidents: They do not automatically receive it. By tradition, an outgoing president may request continued access, and the incoming administration typically grants it for a transition period.[4]
Who produces it
The people who prepare it are not the same as the people who receive it. Staff from the ODNI's PDB staff work overnight to gather analysis from all 18 Intelligence Community elements.[4]
Special cases
Rarely, special editions of the PDB have been "for the president's eyes only," with any further sharing left to the president's discretion.[2]
The brief is also tailored to each president. It is shaped to the way each president likes to absorb information.[3] Some presidents prefer to read it, and others prefer oral briefings.
